definition: Gender digital divide is defined as gender biases coded into technology products, technology sector, and digital skills education.
details: It can refer to women's and other gender identity's use of, and professional development in computing work. The gender digital divide has changed throughout history due to social roles, economics, and educational opportunities. As the gender spectrum continues to exist more prominently in social and professional spaces, the inclusion of other identities is an important area of concern in these types of conversations. These other identities can include any other than cis-gender male. Non-binary people make up a significant portion of the population and their existence is affected by the digital divide nonetheless.

explainer.lead: The gender digital divide describes how gender bias can shape technology products, the technology sector, and digital-skills education. It matters because these biases affect who can use technology, develop computing careers, and influence the products being built.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a club where some children are encouraged to learn building skills and others are left out, so most of the club's creations suit only the encouraged group. The gender digital divide is a similar pattern involving technology, education, and computing jobs. It concerns women, non-binary people, and others who are not cisgender men.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers can use this concept to examine gender bias in product decisions, workplace participation, and pathways into digital skills and computing roles. Reviews should consider professional development as well as technology use, and should not reduce gender to a male/female split. Treating access alone as the whole problem can miss bias in products and workplaces.
tiers.paperLevel: The gender digital divide is defined as gender biases coded into technology products, the technology sector, and digital-skills education. Its scope includes technology use and professional development in computing, with its form changing through social roles, economics, and educational opportunities. It also encompasses non-binary people and other gender identities beyond cisgender men.

explainer.example: Suppose a digital-skills course mostly enrolls cisgender men, and a technology team then develops its workforce largely from that group. Women and non-binary people have fewer opportunities in this pathway, while the team's products and workplace can continue reflecting a narrower range of gender perspectives.

explainer.intuition: The divide is more than a gap in technology use: gender bias can appear in products, workplaces, and routes into digital skills. Its form changes as social roles, economics, and educational opportunities change.
howItWorks: Social roles, economics, and educational opportunities shape access to digital skills.
Gender bias can affect participation and professional development in computing work.
Bias can also be coded into technology products and present in the technology sector.
Women, non-binary people, and other identities beyond cisgender men can experience these effects.
The pattern changes over time rather than remaining fixed.
explainer.whyItMatters: It connects product bias, sector participation, and education instead of treating them as separate issues. Including non-binary and other gender identities makes discussions of digital inequality more representative of the people affected.
misconceptions: It is not limited to whether women and men use technology differently.
It does not treat gender as only two categories; non-binary and other identities are included.
It is not a fixed pattern, because social roles, economics, and educational opportunities change it over time.
